headline: The ROTOR Act would have required more aircraft to carry tracking equipment and tightened limits on military and government exceptions, but it failed.
what_it_does: The bill would have required most aircraft to carry ADS-B In equipment, which shows pilots where other aircraft are and gives traffic alerts. It would have narrowed when government flights, such as training flights, could skip broadcasting their location with ADS-B Out, and added reporting rules for those exceptions. It would have repealed a 2025 law letting certain military helicopters skip ADS-B Out in the Washington, DC, area. It also would have ordered audits and reviews and required the FAA to set up an office to coordinate military use of airspace.

who_it_affects.how: They would generally have had to install and use ADS-B In equipment, which current law does not require.

who_it_affects.group: Military and other government flight crews
who_it_affects.how: Fewer of their flights, such as training flights, could have qualified to skip location broadcasting, and using the exception would have required more reporting and notice.

who_it_affects.group: Military helicopter units in the Washington, DC, area
who_it_affects.how: They would have lost a 2025 exemption from ADS-B Out rules in that region.
It would have had to create a military airspace coordination office, review flight routes around airports, and sign safety information-sharing agreements with military agencies.

who_it_affects.group: Government auditors (GAO and the Transportation and Army inspectors general)
who_it_affects.how: They would have been required to review the exception's use, audit FAA oversight every year, and audit Army coordination with the FAA.
